title: 학술 세미나 토론 표현 / Expressions for academic seminar discussions
bridge: In Korean academic seminars, politeness and hierarchy are reflected in the use of formal registers such as hap-shyo-che (합니다체) and hae-yo-che (해요체), which do not have a direct equivalent in Spanish. Additionally, it is common to use mitigation strategies like '-것 같다' (it seems that) and '-는데' (but) to soften opinions, whereas in Spanish we tend to be more direct with phrases like 'yo creo' or 'en mi opinión'. Be careful not to translate the Spanish 'pero' literally as '하지만' in debate contexts, since in Korean '-는데' is preferred to link contrasting ideas without being abrupt.
rule: To participate in a Korean academic seminar at a C1 level, it is essential to master: 1) Formal register: verb endings such as -습니다/ㅂ니다, -습니까? for questions, and -아/어요 for a semi-formal tone. 2) Mitigated opinion expressions: -다고 생각합니다 (I think that), -다고 볼 수 있습니다 (it can be considered that), -것 같습니다 (it seems that). 3) Contrast and concession connectors: -지만, -는데, -에도 불구하고 (despite). 4) Turn-taking formulas: 실례지만 (excuse me), 한 가지 의견을 말씀드리겠습니다 (I would like to share an opinion). 5) To agree or disagree: 동의합니다 (I agree), 동의하기 어렵습니다 (it is difficult to agree). 6) To reformulate: 다시 말하면 (in other words), 즉 (that is), 바꿔 말하면 (put differently). 7) To summarize: 요약하자면 (to summarize), 결론적으로 (in conclusion). Remember that in Korean the verb goes at the end and subjects are often omitted if clear. Also, in academic contexts, the use of '너' (you) is avoided, and titles or '교수님' are used instead.

concept_examples.text: 제 생각에는 이 이론이 타당하다고 생각합니다.
concept_examples.translation: In my opinion, this theory is valid.
concept_examples.phonetic: [tɕe sɛŋɡaɡe̞nɯn i iɾoɲi tʰa̠da̠ŋɦa̠da̠ɡo̞ sʰɛŋɡa̠kʰa̠mnida̠]

concept_examples.text: 그 점에 대해서는 동의하기 어렵습니다.
concept_examples.translation: Regarding that point, I find it difficult to agree.
concept_examples.phonetic: [kɯ tɕ͈ʌ̹me̞ te̞ɦa̠sʰʌ̹nɯn to̞ŋɰiɦa̠ɡi ʌ̹ɾjʌ̹psʰɯmnida̠]

concept_examples.text: 다시 말하면, 이 결과는 연구 가설을 지지한다고 볼 수 있습니다.
concept_examples.translation: In other words, this result can be considered to support the research hypothesis.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ta̠ɕʰi ma̠ɽɯɕʰjʌ̹n, i kjʌ̹ɡwa̠nɯn jʌ̹nɡu ka̠sʰɜ̝rɯɭ t͡ɕid͡ʑiɦa̠nda̠ɡo̞ po̞ɭ sʰu ĭssʰɯmnida̠]

concept_examples.text: 요약하자면, 추가적인 연구가 필요합니다.
concept_examples.translation: To summarize, additional research is needed.
concept_examples.phonetic: [jo̞ja̠kʰa̠d͡ʑa̠mjʌ̹n, t͡ɕʰuɡa̠d͡ʑʌ̹ɡin jʌ̹nɡuɡa̠ pʰiɾjo̞ɦa̠mnida̠]

common_error.wrong: 제 생각에는 이 이론이 타당하지만, 그러나 다른 의견도 있습니다.
common_error.correct: 제 생각에는 이 이론이 타당하지만, 다른 의견도 있습니다.
common_error.correct_alt: 제 생각에는 이 이론이 타당한데, 다른 의견도 있습니다.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, it is common to use 'pero' after a concession, but in Korean '하지만' and '그러나' are redundant if '-지만' is already used with the verb. When combining '-지만' (which already means 'but'), you should not add another connector like '그러나' or '하지만'. Use only one. You can also use '-는데' for a softer contrast in spoken contexts.

examples.original: 제 견해로는 이 접근법이 효과적입니다.
examples.phonetic: [tɕe̞ kjʌ̹nɦe̞ɾo̞nɯn i t͡ɕʌ̹p̚k͈ɯnbʌ̞bi hjogwa̠d͡ʑʌ̹ɡimnida̠]
examples.translation: From my perspective, this approach is effective.
examples.note: Use '제 견해로는' for a formal register. In Spanish, we say 'desde mi punto de vista', but in Korean '제 생각에는' is more natural in conversation.

examples.original: 이 부분에 대해서는 다른 시각이 있을 수 있다고 생각합니다.
examples.phonetic: [i puɦa̠ŋe̞ te̞ɦa̠sʰʌ̹nɯn ta̠ɾɯn ɕʰiɡa̠ɡi ĭssʰɯɭ sʰu ĭttɕ͈a̠ɡo̞ sʰɛŋɡa̠kʰa̠mnida̠]
examples.translation: Regarding this part, I think there may be other perspectives.
examples.note: The structure '-을 수 있다' (there may be) is useful for showing openness. In Spanish, we use 'puede que', but in Korean '-을 수 있다' is preferred.

examples.original: 저는 그 주장에 전적으로 동의합니다.
examples.phonetic: [t͡ɕʌ̹nɯn kɯ t͡ɕuɟ͡ʑa̠ŋe̞ t͡ɕʌ̹ɲd͡ʑʌ̹k̚ɯɾo̞ to̞ŋɰiɦa̠mnida̠]
examples.translation: I fully agree with that claim.
examples.note: '전적으로' means 'fully'. In Spanish, 'de acuerdo' functions as an adjective, but in Korean the verb '동의하다' is used.

examples.original: 그 관점을 존중하지만, 저는 다른 의견을 가지고 있습니다.
examples.phonetic: [kɯ kwa̠nɲd͡ʑʌ̹mɯɭ t͡ɕo̞ɲd͡ʑuŋɦa̠d͡ʑiɱa̠n, t͡ɕʌ̹nɯn ta̠ɾɯn ɰiɡjʌ̹nɯɭ ka̠d͡ʑiɡo̞ ĭssʰɯmnida̠]
examples.translation: I respect that viewpoint, but I have a different opinion.
examples.note: Using '존중하지만' (I respect but) is a polite way to start a disagreement. In Spanish, we sometimes say 'respeto tu opinión, pero'.

examples.original: 이 논리에는 몇 가지 문제점이 있다고 생각합니다.
examples.phonetic: [i no̞ɭɭi.e̞nɯn mjʌ̹t̚k͈a̠d͡ʑi mʌ̹ɲd͡ʑe̞d͡ʑʌ̹mi ĭttɕ͈a̠ɡo̞ sʰɛŋɡa̠kʰa̠mnida̠]
examples.translation: I think there are several issues with this logic.
examples.note: In academic contexts, '문제점' (issue) is used instead of '문제' (problem) for specificity. In Spanish, 'problema' serves both meanings.

examples.original: 바꿔 말하면, 이 결과는 다른 방식으로 해석될 수 있습니다.
examples.phonetic: [pa̠k͈wʌ̹ ma̠ɽɯɕʰjʌ̹n, i kjʌ̹ɡwa̠nɯn ta̠ɾɯn pa̠ŋɕʰiɡɯɾo̞ hɛ̝sʰʌ̹k̚t͈we̞ɭ sʰu ĭssʰɯmnida̠]
examples.translation: Put differently, this result can be interpreted in another way.
examples.note: '바꿔 말하면' is the formula for 'put differently'. It is common in both Spanish and Korean.

examples.original: 종합해 보면, 이 연구는 중요한 시사점을 제공합니다.
examples.phonetic: [t͡ɕo̞ŋɦa̠pʰɛ̝ po̞mjʌ̹n, i jʌ̹nɡunɯn t͡ɕuŋjo̞ɦa̠n ɕʰisʰa̠d͡ʑʌ̹mɯɭ t͡ɕe̞ɡo̞ŋɦa̠mnida̠]
examples.translation: On balance, this research provides important insights.
examples.note: '종합해 보면' is ideal for beginning a general conclusion. In Spanish, we use 'en síntesis'.

examples.original: 결론적으로, 이론과 실제 사이에 간극이 존재합니다.
examples.phonetic: [kjʌ̹ɭɭo̞ɲd͡ʑʌ̹ɡɯɾo̞, iɾo̞nɡwa̠ ɕʰiɭd͡ʑe̞ sʰa̠i.e̞ ka̠nɡɯɡi t͡ɕo̞ɲd͡ʑe̞ɦa̠mnida̠]
examples.translation: In conclusion, there is a gap between theory and practice.
examples.note: '결론적으로' is the direct formula. At a C1 level, you can also use '결론을 내리자면' (if I must conclude).

examples.original: 마지막으로, 이러한 논의를 바탕으로 향후 연구 방향을 제안하고 싶습니다.
examples.phonetic: [ma̠d͡ʑĭma̠ɡɯɾo̞, iɾʌ̹ɦa̠n no̞ɲɰiɾɯɭ pa̠tʰa̠ŋɯɾo̞ hjʌ̹ŋɦu jʌ̹nɡu pa̠ŋʝja̠ŋɯɭ t͡ɕe̞a̠nɦa̠ɡo̞ ɕʰip͈sʰɯmnida̠]
examples.translation: Finally, I would like to propose future research directions based on this discussion.
examples.note: The construction '-을 바탕으로' (based on) is typical of academic registers. In Spanish, we use 'basándonos en'.

title: 고급 직장 내 커뮤니케이션 / Professional communication at a high level
bridge: In Korean, politeness and hierarchy are expressed through verb endings and specific vocabulary, whereas in Spanish we mainly use the 'usted' form and polite phrases. A common mistake is transferring the direct structure from Spanish to Korean, resulting in a tone that is too abrupt or informal. Additionally, Korean has the honorific '시' which is inserted into the verb, something that has no direct equivalent in Spanish. Mastering these nuances is key to communicating with respect in professional Korean environments.
rule: In formal Korean, the endings '-습니다/ㅂ니다' are used for standard formal speech and '-어요/아요' for polite informal speech. In professional contexts, it is essential to use the formal register '합쇼체' ('-습니다') with superiors and clients. Additionally, the honorific suffix '-시-' is used after the verb root when speaking to or about someone of higher status (e.g., 가시다, 보시다). To express polite requests, '-어 주시겠어요?' or '-아/어 드릴까요?' (offer) are used. Expressions like '실례합니다' (excuse me), '수고하셨습니다' (good job), and '말씀' (honorific form of '말' meaning 'speech') are also common. Avoid using informal forms like '반말' in professional settings unless there is a relationship of great trust and clear hierarchy. Note that Korean has no grammatical gender, but choosing the correct register is crucial.

concept_examples.text: 회의 일정을 조정해 주시겠어요?
concept_examples.translation: Could you adjust the meeting schedule?
concept_examples.phonetic: /hø.i il.t͈ɕəŋ.ɨl tɕo.dʑʌŋ.hɛ dʑu.ɕi.ɡe.s'ʌ.jo?/

concept_examples.text: 수고하셨습니다. 다음에 또 연락드리겠습니다.
concept_examples.translation: You’ve done a great job. I’ll contact you again in the future.
concept_examples.phonetic: /su.ɡo.ha.ɕjʌt.s'ɯm.ni.da. ta.ɯm.e t͈o jʌn.rak.tɯ.ri.ɡet.s'ɯm.ni.da./

concept_examples.text: 그 부분에 대해서는 제가 확인 후 말씀드리겠습니다.
concept_examples.translation: Regarding that point, I will inform you after verifying it.
concept_examples.phonetic: /kɯ pu.bu.nɛ dɛ.hɛ.s'ɔ.nɯn tɕe.ɡa hwak.in hu mal.s'ɯm.tɯ.ri.ɡet.s'ɯm.ni.da./

concept_examples.text: 실례합니다, 지금 통화 괜찮으신가요?
concept_examples.translation: Excuse me, is this a good time to talk?
concept_examples.phonetic: /ɕil.lje.ham.ni.da, tɕi.ɡɯm tʰoŋ.hwa kwɛn.tɕ'an.ɯ.ɕin.ɡa.jo?/

common_error.correct_alt: 회의 일정을 조정해 주실 수 있으신가요?
common_error.explanation: The form '-주세요' is polite, but in a professional setting with a superior or client, it can sound too direct. It is preferable to use '-주시겠어요?' or '-주실 수 있으신가요?' as they are more indirect and express greater respect, similar to using the conditional in Spanish: '¿Podría...?' instead of 'Haga...'.

examples.original: 의견이 있으시면 자유롭게 말씀해 주세요.
examples.phonetic: /ɰi.ɡjʌ.ni it.s'ɯ.ɕi.mjʌn tɕa.ju.rop.k'e mal.s'ɯ.mɛ dʑu.se.jo./
examples.translation: If you have any opinions, please feel free to express them.
examples.note: Use of '말씀하다' (honorific form of 'to speak') and '-세요' to give permission.

examples.original: 그 안건에 대해서는 다음 회의에서 논의하도록 하겠습니다.
examples.phonetic: /kɯ an.ɡʌ.nɛ dɛ.hɛ.s'ɔ.nɯn ta.ɯm hø.i.e.s'ɔ no.ɰi.ha.do.rok ha.ɡet.s'ɯm.ni.da./
examples.translation: Regarding that point, we will discuss it in the next meeting.
examples.note: The structure '-도록 하겠습니다' expresses formal intention or decision.

examples.original: 시간을 내주셔서 감사합니다.
examples.phonetic: /ɕi.ɡa.nɯl nɛ.dʑu.ɕjɔ.s'ɔ kam.sa.ham.ni.da./
examples.translation: Thank you for taking the time to meet with us.
examples.note: Formal thanks using '내주시다' (honorific of 'to dedicate').

examples.original: 첨부된 문서를 확인하시고 회신 부탁드립니다.
examples.phonetic: /tɕʰʌm.bu.dwen mun.s'ɔ.rɨl hwa.k'in.ha.ɕi.ɡo hø.ɕin pu.tʰak.tɯ.rim.ni.da./
examples.translation: Please review the attached document and reply.
examples.note: Use of '부탁드립니다' (humble form of 'to ask').

examples.original: 제안서를 검토해 주시면 감사하겠습니다.
examples.phonetic: /tɕe.an.s'ɔ.rɨl kʌm.tʰo.hɛ dʑu.ɕi.mjʌn kam.sa.ha.ɡet.s'ɯm.ni.da./
examples.translation: I would appreciate it if you could review the proposal.
examples.note: Polite conditional with '-면 감사하겠습니다' to express a request.

examples.original: 이 메일은 회의록을 공유드리기 위해 보내드립니다.
examples.phonetic: /i me.il.ɯn hø.i.rok.ɯl koŋ.ju.tɯ.ri.ɡi.ɥi.hɛ po.nɛ.tɯ.rim.ni.da./
examples.translation: This email is to share the meeting minutes with you.
examples.note: Humble verbs: '공유드리다' and '보내드리다'.

examples.original: 저희가 제안한 조건을 한번 더 고려해 주시길 바랍니다.
examples.phonetic: /tɕʌ.hi.ɡa tɕe.an.han tɕo.ɡɔ.nɨl han.bʌn tɔ ko.ɾjɔ.hɛ dʑu.ɕi.kil pa.rap.ni.da./
examples.translation: We ask that you consider our proposed conditions one more time.
examples.note: Structure '-시길 바랍니다' for formal requests.

examples.original: 솔직히 말씀드리면, 이 부분은 개선이 필요할 것 같습니다.
examples.phonetic: /sol.tɕik.hi mal.s'ɯm.tɯ.ri.mjʌn, i pu.bu.nɯn kɛ.s'ɛ.ni pʰi.jo.ɦal kʌt kat.s'ɯm.ni.da./
examples.translation: To be honest, I think this part needs improvement.
examples.note: Opinion expression with '것 같습니다' to soften criticism.

examples.original: 이 조건이라면 저희로서는 수용하기 어렵습니다.
examples.phonetic: /i tɕo.ɡʌ.ni.ra.mjʌn tɕʌ.hi.ro.s'ɔ.nɯn su.joŋ.ha.ɡi ʌ.ɾjʌp.s'ɯm.ni.da./
examples.translation: Under these conditions, it would be difficult for us to accept.
examples.note: Use of '어렵다' to indirectly decline.

title: 문학적 분석과 문화적 코드 해독 / Literary analysis and cultural codes
bridge: In Spanish, when analyzing literature or culture, we use discourse markers and connectors like 'desde una perspectiva', 'en cierto modo', or 'cabe destacar'. In Korean, these nuances are conveyed not only through specific vocabulary but also through modal particles, levels of formality, and suffixes that mark the speaker's attitude (e.g., -군요, -잖아요, -거든요). Additionally, literary Korean tends to be more indirect and relies on cultural context (Confucianism, social hierarchy), which requires interpreting silences and elisions. For Spanish speakers, the challenge is not to over-explain and to learn to read between the lines.
rule: To express literary or cultural analysis in Korean at a C1 level, you must master: 1) Analysis connectors: -(으)므로 (therefore), -에도 불구하고 (despite), -을/를 고려하면 (considering that), -에 비추어 볼 때 (in light of). 2) Modal particles that nuance opinions: -군요 (surprise/confirmation), -잖아요 (shared reason), -거든요 (personal explanation), -나 보다 (it seems like). 3) The use of '한국적' (Korean) vs '보편적' (universal) to contrast perspectives. 4) Indirect quotes with -다고 하다, -냐고 하다, -라고 하다 to reference works or authors. 5) Formal register (합쇼체) in essays and semi-formal register (해요체) in academic conversation. Furthermore, the use of contractions and elisions typical of educated spoken discourse (e.g., '그니까', '말이죠') is essential for sounding native.

concept_examples.text: 이 소설은 사회적 모순을 비판하는 동시에 인간의 보편적 정서를 탐구한다.
concept_examples.translation: This novel criticizes social contradictions while also exploring the universal emotions of humanity.
concept_examples.phonetic: [i sʰosʰɔɾɯn sʰa̠d͡ʑʌ̹k̚ mo̞sʰuɲɯɭ pʰibipʰa̠nɦa̠nɯn to̞ŋɕʰie̞ inɟa̠nɰi po̞pʰjʌ̹nɟʌ̹k̚ cʰɥʌ̹ŋsʰɜ̝ɭ tʰa̠mɡuɦa̠nda̠]

concept_examples.text: 작가의 의도와 무관하게 독자는 작품에서 새로운 의미를 발견하게 된다.
concept_examples.translation: Regardless of the author's intent, the reader ends up discovering new meanings in the work.
concept_examples.phonetic: [t͡ɕa̠k̚k͈a̠ɰi ɰido̞wa̠ muɡwa̠nɦa̠ɡe̞ to̞k̚t͡ɕa̠nɯn t͡ɕa̠k̚pʰɥim e̞sʰʌ̹ sʰɛ̝ɾo̞ɯn ɰimiɾɯɭ pa̠ɭɡjʌ̹nɦa̠ɡe̞ twe̞nda̠]

concept_examples.text: 이 작품은 한국 전쟁의 트라우마를 세대를 초월한 보편적 주제로 승화시킨다.
concept_examples.translation: This work sublimates the trauma of the Korean War into a universal theme that transcends generations.
concept_examples.phonetic: [i t͡ɕa̠k̚pʰɯmɯn ha̠nɡuk̚ t͡ɕʌ̹ɲd͡ʑɛ̝ŋɰi tʰɯɾa̠uma̠ɾɯɭ sʰe̞dɛ̝ɾɯɭ cʰo̞ʷʌ̹nɦa̠n po̞pʰjʌ̹nɟʌ̹k̚ t͡ɕut͡ɕe̞ɾo̞ sʰɯŋɦwa̠ɕʰik͈inda̠]

concept_examples.text: 문화적 코드를 이해하지 못하면 은유의 깊이를 놓치기 쉽다.
concept_examples.translation: Without understanding cultural codes, it is easy to miss the depth of metaphor.
concept_examples.phonetic: [munβwa̠d͡ʑʌ̹k̚ kʰo̞dɯɾɯɭ iɦɛ̝ɦa̠d͡ʑi mo̞tʰa̠mjʌ̹n ɯnɲuɰi kipʰiɾɯɭ no̞t̚t͡ɕʰiɡi ɕʰɥip̚t͈a̠]

common_error.wrong: 저는 이 책을 읽었어요, 그리고 인상깊었어요. 작가가 사회 문제를 보여줘요.
common_error.correct: 이 책을 읽고 상당히 인상 깊었습니다. 작가가 사회 문제를 비판하고 있는 것으로 보입니다.
common_error.correct_alt: 이 책을 읽으면서 사회 문제에 대한 작가의 비판적 시각이 두드러진다고 느꼈습니다.
common_error.explanation: The typical error is using a simple spoken structure (I + verb + and + verb) without analytical nuances. In academic Korean, avoid repeating the explicit subject, use connectors like '-고' instead of '그리고', and employ expressions like '-고 있는 것으로 보입니다' to sound analytical. Additionally, '보여줘요' is too literal; '비판하다' (to criticize) or '드러내다' (to reveal) are preferred.

examples.original: 이 시는 겨울을 죽음으로 은유하며, 동시에 재생의 가능성을 암시한다.
examples.phonetic: [i ɕʰi nɯn kjʌ̹uɽɯɭ t͡ɕuɡɯmɯɾo̞ ɯnɲuɦa̠mjʌ̹, to̞ŋɕʰie̞ t͡ɕɛ̝sʰɛ̝ŋɰi ka̠nɯŋsʰʌ̹ŋɯɭ a̠mɕʰiɦa̠nda̠]
examples.translation: This poem metaphorizes winter as death and simultaneously hints at the possibility of rebirth.
examples.note: The structure 'A를 B로 은유하다' (to metaphorize A as B) is used. Note that explicit subjects are often unnecessary.

examples.original: 작품 곳곳에 나타난 불의 이미지는 열정과 파괴의 이중성을 지닌다.

examples.translation: While the author's early works deal with personal awakening, the later ones question social structures.
examples.note: The use of '-반면' (whereas) and the idiomatic expression '문제 삼다' (to question), which is more natural than '비판하다'.

title: 철학적 사고와 추상적 추론 / Philosophical and abstract reasoning
bridge: In Korean, expressing philosophical and abstract nuances relies on nominalizing structures such as -기, -음, and modal particles like -ㄴ/은/는 것, which convert complete propositions into nouns. Unlike Spanish, which uses subordinate clauses with 'que' or infinitives (e.g., 'el hecho de que...', 'que exista...'), Korean prefers direct nominalization of the verb or adjective. This means the verb is not conjugated for person or tense in the nominalized part; instead, temporal and modal information is added at the end of the sentence. Spanish speakers tend to translate 'que' literally as '것' or '기' without considering that these particles have specific uses: -기 is more abstract and general, while -(으)ㅁ is more formal and emphasizes a completed fact.
rule:
To express abstract propositions, three main nominalizers are used:
1. -기 (simple and abstract nominalization): used to refer to the activity itself (e.g., '무엇을 안다는 것' vs '아는 것'). It combines with verbs and adjectives.
2. -(으)ㅁ (formal and factual nominalization): used in written, academic, or formal contexts. It indicates that the proposition is a fact or truth. Example: '그가 옳음은 명백하다' (that he is right is obvious).
3. -ㄴ/은/는 것 (nominalization with the nuance of 'the fact that'): used in more colloquial contexts and is similar to a complementizer. It can carry past, present, or future tense.
Additionally, for hypothetical or abstract reasoning, the suppositional mood -ㄴ/은/는지 (if) or -다면/라면 (if... then) is used. Logical connectors such as -므로 (therefore), -에도 불구하고 (despite), -면 (if) are also employed to build complex arguments.
At the C1 level, students are expected to use these resources fluently to debate, express nuanced opinions, and formulate hypotheses. Attention must be paid to register: in informal philosophical conversation, -기 and -는 것 are preferred; in essays or formal speeches, -(으)ㅁ and -므로 are used.

common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers often mistakenly use '것' as a catch-all translation for 'que', but in Korean, when the main verb is 'pensar' (생각하다) or 'decir' (말하다), the complementizer -다고 is used instead of -는 것. '것' is used to nominalize the object of verbs of knowledge, not for verbs of opinion or communication. Another common variant is using '-는 것' with verbs like 'saber' (알다) or 'creer' (믿다), but with 'pensar' (생각하다), -다고 is preferred. The correct form is '어렵다고 생각해요' (I think it's difficult).

examples.translation: If free will does not exist, moral responsibility cannot be established either.
examples.note: The particle -ㄴ다면 expresses a hypothetical condition, and -도 means 'also'.

examples.original: 인식의 한계를 인정한다면, 우리는 더 열린 사고를 가질 수 있다.

examples.translation: If we acknowledge the limits of knowledge, we can have more open-minded thinking.
examples.note: The particle -면 expresses real conditions, and -ㄹ 수 있다 indicates possibility.

examples.original: 어떤 사람들은 윤리가 보편적이라고 주장하지만, 이는 문화에 따라 달라질 수 있다.

title: 고급 사회정치적 논평 / Advanced sociopolitical commentary
bridge: In Korean, unlike Spanish, modality and evidentiality are often expressed through verbal suffixes that indicate whether the information is firsthand (-더라), inferred (-겠-), or cited (-다고). While Spanish uses the subjunctive and modal verbs (parece que, dicen que, debió de ser), Korean integrates these notions directly into the verb. For a Spanish speaker, the challenge is not to translate 'dicen que' literally with an explicit subject, but to use forms like -다고 하다. Additionally, Korean lacks articles and formal distinctions between singular and plural in nouns, but markers like -들 and topic particles (은/는) add nuances of contrast and emphasis that have no direct equivalent in Spanish.
rule: For advanced sociopolitical commentary in Korean (C1 level), precise use is expected of: (1) evidentiality and citation markers: -다고 하다 (it is said that), -다는 주장 (the claim that), -다고 보다 (to consider that), -라고 평가하다 (to evaluate as). (2) Forms of inference and conjecture: -겠-, -을/ㄹ 것 같다, -나 보다. (3) Logical connectors for contrast and cause: -(으)나 (but), -에도 불구하고 (despite), -므로 (due to), -는 한 (insofar as). (4) Passive and causative constructions for objective analysis: -아/어지다, -게 하다. (5) Topic particles (은/는) to mark contrast between political stances. Additionally, mastery of the formal register -습니다/습니까 and the use of Sino-Korean vocabulary (한자어) such as 담론 (discourse), 정책 (policy), 입장 (stance), etc., is required. Common mistakes: omitting the citation marker when paraphrasing a politician; using informal forms in formal debate contexts; and failing to distinguish between -다고 (direct citation) and -라고 (direct citation with speech verbs), which are actually used interchangeably but with nuances.

common_error.wrong: 정부는 말해요 이 법은 나쁜 예요.
common_error.explanation: A typical error for Spanish speakers is translating 'the government says this law is bad' using the direct word order of Spanish and omitting the citation construction -다고. In Korean, indirect citation always comes before the verb, and the final verb must be in the appropriate form (here, formal -합니다). Additionally, -다고 말하다 or -라고 하다 are commonly used. To avoid this mistake, remember the structure: subject + citation (with -다고) + speech verb (말하다, 주장하다, 평가하다). It is also common to confuse the topic particle (은/는) with the subject particle (이/가); in this context, '정부는' marks the topic.

title: 복합적 개인 서사 / Complex personal narratives
bridge: In Spanish, when narrating past experiences, we often alternate between the preterite indefinite and imperfect to situate the action in time and describe the context. In Korean, this distinction is not marked by verb tenses but by aspect and connectors that express simultaneity, causality, or contrast. Additionally, Korean uses indirect quotation structures and expressions of personal reflection that have no direct equivalent in Spanish, forcing the speaker to reorganize the information. The biggest challenge for a Spanish speaker is letting go of the need to mark tense in every verb and relying on discourse markers to convey sequence and perspective.
rule: To narrate complex personal stories in Korean at a C1 level, several resources are used: 1) **Sequence connectors**: -고 나서 (after), -아/어서 (and then), -다가 (while doing something that gets interrupted), -면서 (while). 2) **Cause/contrast connectors**: -기 때문에 (because), -지만 (but), -는데 (whereas, context). 3) **Indirect quotation for thoughts/emotions**: -다고 생각하다, -다고 느끼다, -다고 말하다. 4) **Reflection expressions**: -ㄴ/는 셈이다 (it's as if), -ㄴ/는 법이다 (it's typical that), -ㄹ 뻔했다 (I almost). 5) **Progressive and perfect aspect**: -고 있었다 (was doing), -아/어 있었다 (had been). 6) **Informal oral register** for narrating to friends: -잖아, -거든, -더라. Unlike Spanish, the base tense is established at the beginning of the narrative (일반적으로 과거 시제로 시작) and then maintained through context, occasionally using the historical present for vividness. It is crucial to master the alternation between formal and informal forms depending on the interlocutor, and the use of modal particles such as -지, -네, -군 to express surprise or discovery.

title: 고급 토론 · 반박 기술 / Advanced Debate and Refutation Techniques
bridge: In Spanish, refutation often relies on discourse connectors and verbal nuances (e.g., 'sin embargo', 'no obstante', 'si bien es cierto que...'). In Korean, this function is primarily achieved through verb endings that express concession, contrast, and condition, along with emphatic particles like 은/는 or 도. Additionally, Korean marks respect and politeness through speech levels, which do not exist in Spanish. To debate at a C1 level, you must master structures like '-기는 하지만', '-는 한', '-ㄴ/는 반면에', and know when to use the formal register '-습니다' or the semi-formal '-아/어요'. Beware: Spanish speakers tend to directly translate 'aunque + subjunctive' structures, but Korean uses verbal suffixes with specific nuances.
rule: For advanced Korean debate (C1), the following structures are used: (1) Concession and contrast: '-기는 하지만' (although, conceding that...), '-는다고 해도' (even if...), '-는 반면에' (while, on the other hand). (2) Conditions and limits: '-는 한' (insofar as, as long as), '-지 않는 한' (unless). (3) Emphasis and nuance: particles like '은/는' to contrast topics, '도' for inclusion. (4) Direct refutation with '아니다' (it is not) and structures like '-라고 볼 수 없다' (it cannot be considered that). (5) Register: in formal debates '-습니다/ㅂ니다' is used, and in semi-formal contexts '-아/어요'. There is no direct equivalent to the Spanish subjunctive, so concessions are expressed with verb endings. Additionally, Korean has particles that mark the speaker's attitude: '잖아요' (as you know), '거든요' (explanation). In debates, '-ㄴ/는데' is used to set context before counter-arguing.

title: 학술적 어휘 표현 / Academic specialized vocabulary
bridge: In academic Korean, unlike Spanish, many nouns of Chinese origin (한자어) are often combined with the verb 하다 to form verbs. The passive voice with -되다 and formal structures without a direct equivalent in Spanish, such as the suffix -에 따르면 ('according to'), are also common. Furthermore, academic Korean tends to be more nominalized than Spanish, so Spanish speakers should avoid literal translations of verbs like 'analizar' (to analyze) or 'proponer' (to propose).
rule: In Korean academic register, Chinese-origin nouns (한자어) combine with 하다 to form active verbs, with 되다 for passive forms, and with 시키다 for causatives. For example: 연구하다 (to research), 연구되다 (to be researched), 연구시키다 (to have someone research). To express 'according to,' use -에 따르면, and for 'with respect to,' use -에 관하여. It is crucial to maintain the SOV word order and use particles such as 은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서 correctly. In formal contexts, endings like -(ㄴ/는)다, -(ㄴ/는)지, -(ㄴ/는)것이다 are used. Avoid mixing levels of formality.

examples.note: The ending -한다 (해라체) is typical of academic writing and news.

examples.original: 결론적으로, 본 연구는 새로운 시사점을 제기한다.
examples.phonetic: [kjʌ̹ɭʎo̞ɲd͡ʑʌ̹k̚ɯɾo̞ po̞n jʌ̹nɡuːn sʰe̞ɾo̞un ɕiɕa̠d͡ʑʌ̹mɯɭ t͡ɕe̞ɡiɦa̠nda̠]
examples.translation: In conclusion, this study raises new implications.
examples.note: Use of '결론적으로' (conclusively) and verb '제기하다' (to raise).

title: 속어와 관용적 표현 / Idioms and colloquial expressions
bridge: In Spanish, we often use idioms like 'estar en las nubes' (to be daydreaming) or 'tirar la toalla' (to give up) to express ideas figuratively. In Korean, there are equally vivid expressions with different imagery that lose their meaning if translated literally. Additionally, Korean uses particles and speech levels that affect register: most idioms are used in 반말 (informal speech) or 존댓말 (formal speech), but switching between them without mastery can sound odd. As a Spanish speaker, your challenge will be to avoid literal translations and grasp the cultural nuances of these expressions.
rule: In Korean, idioms (관용구) are fixed phrases whose meaning cannot be deduced from the individual words. They often originate from culture, history, or daily life. They are used in both informal conversation (반말) and formal speech (존댓말), though some expressions are more colloquial. To form sentences with these idioms, they are combined with verbs like 하다 (to do) or 되다 (to become), and often constructed with particles such as 이/가 or 을/를. It is crucial to respect the word order and the context of use. At the C1 level, you should recognize and use these idioms in appropriate situations, varying the register according to the interlocutor. Be careful with expressions that sound too informal in formal contexts.

concept_examples.text: 그 사람은 입이 가볍지 않아요.
concept_examples.translation: That person doesn’t have a light mouth (they aren’t gossipy).
concept_examples.phonetic: [kɯ sʰaɾamɯn ibi kapjʌpchi antʰa̠jo]

concept_examples.text: 오늘은 눈이 높아서 뭐 먹고 싶은 게 없어.
concept_examples.translation: Today I have high standards, so I don’t feel like eating anything.
concept_examples.phonetic: [onɯɾɯn nuni nopʰa̠sʰʌ mwʌ mʌkko ɕipʰɯn ke ʌpsʌ]

concept_examples.text: 그 친구는 항상 콧대가 높아.
concept_examples.translation: That friend always has a high nose (they’re arrogant).
concept_examples.phonetic: [kɯ tɕʰingu nɯn haŋsʰaŋ kʰot̚tɛga nopʰa̠]

concept_examples.text: 걱정 마, 내가 다리를 놓아 줄게.
concept_examples.translation: Don’t worry, I’ll build a bridge (I’ll act as an intermediary).
concept_examples.phonetic: [kʌdʑʌŋ ma, nɛga taɾɯɾɯn noa̠ tɕulɡe]

common_error.wrong: 나는 오늘 물이 많아서 기분이 좋아.
common_error.correct: 나는 오늘 물이 많아서? -> 나는 오늘 물이 올라서 기분이 좋아.
common_error.explanation: The error comes from literally translating the Spanish expression 'estar en el agua' or confusing idioms. In Korean, '물이 올랐다' (the water rises) means 'to be in a good mood' or 'to have energy,' but '물이 많다' (there is a lot of water) has no figurative meaning. To avoid this mistake, memorize idioms as complete units and pay attention to the verb that accompanies them. Also, do not use '물이 좋다' for this, because it means the water tastes good (to drink).

examples.original: 입이 무겁다
examples.phonetic: [ibi muɡʌp̚t͈a̠]
examples.translation: To have a heavy mouth (to be discreet, not to reveal secrets).
examples.note: Opposite of 입이 가볍다 (light mouth, gossipy). Use it to praise someone who keeps secrets.

examples.original: 눈이 높다
examples.phonetic: [nuni nopʰt͈a̠]
examples.translation: To have high eyes (to be picky or demanding, especially in tastes or partners).
examples.note: Can refer to high standards in general or to someone who is too demanding to find a partner.

examples.original: 손이 크다
examples.phonetic: [soni kʰɯda̠]
examples.translation: To have big hands (to be generous, to spend a lot).
examples.note: Used to describe someone who gives expensive gifts or is extravagant. Do not confuse with the Spanish 'hábil con las manos' (skillful hands).

examples.original: 귀가 얇다
examples.phonetic: [kɥiga̠ jaltʰa̠]
examples.translation: To have thin ears (to be easily influenced, gullible).
examples.note: Similar to the Spanish 'entrarle por los oídos.' Used for someone who is easily convinced.

examples.original: 소 잃고 외양간 고친다
examples.phonetic: [so ilkʰo œjaŋɡan kotɕʰinda̠]
examples.translation: To lose the cow and fix the barn (too late, after the disaster).
examples.note: Equivalent to 'locking the barn door after the horse has bolted.' Used to criticize belated actions.

examples.original: 개미 다리에 고추장 묻히기
examples.phonetic: [kæmi taɾie̞ kodʑudʑaŋ mutʰiɡi]
examples.translation: To put chili paste on an ant’s legs (something absurd and disproportionate).
examples.note: Expresses doing something useless or exaggerated for a small problem. Similar to the Spanish 'to kill a fly with a cannon'.

examples.original: 용이 물 깊은 데 간다
examples.phonetic: [joŋi mul kipʰɯn te̞ kanda̠]
examples.translation: The dragon goes where the water is deep (talented people seek environments where they can thrive).
examples.note: Used to describe someone brilliant who moves toward a suitable setting.

examples.original: 지렁이도 밟으면 꿈틀한다
examples.phonetic: [tɕiɾʌŋido̞ palpʰɯmjʌn kkumtʰɯɾɦanda̠]
examples.translation: Even a worm wriggles if you step on it (even the most patient person gets fed up).
examples.note: Equivalent to 'patience has a limit.' Useful to warn that someone’s patience should not be pushed too far.

examples.original: 밀가루만 보면 체한다
examples.phonetic: [milɡaɾuman po̞mjʌn tɕʰe̞ɦanda̠]
examples.translation: If I only see flour, I get indigestion (to be fed up with something, to have an aversion).
examples.note: Used when someone is tired of something, especially a repetitive situation.

examples.original: 물이 좋다
examples.phonetic: [muri tɕo̞tʰa̠]
examples.translation: The water is good (there’s a good atmosphere, everything is going well).
examples.note: In colloquial context, it can refer to a good general atmosphere or everything being favorable.

examples.original: 다리를 놓다
examples.phonetic: [taɾɯɾɯn no̞tʰa̠]
examples.translation: To build a bridge (to act as an intermediary, to connect people).
examples.note: Similar to the Spanish 'hacer de puente' or 'acercar posturas.' Used in negotiations or introductions.

examples.original: 분위기가 심상치 않다
examples.phonetic: [punɥiɡa̠ ɕimsaŋtɕʰi antʰa̠]
examples.translation: The atmosphere is not normal (you can feel something bad is about to happen).
examples.note: Useful to describe a tense or suspicious situation. Used in informal conversations.

translations.en: Authentic use of colloquial language and idioms

title: 완벽한 유창성: 한국어의 함축적 뉘앙스와 간접 표현 / Native-like fluency: implicit nuances and indirect expressions
bridge: In Spanish, we tend to be explicit with qualifiers like 'perhaps', 'I suppose' or 'I don't know if...'. At a C1 level of Korean, near-native fluency depends on mastering verb endings that carry modal meaning without needing additional words: -거든요, -잖아요, -더라고요, -나 보다, -ㄴ/는 모양이다, among others. The big contrast with Spanish is that these final particles have no direct equivalent; instead, they modify the shared assumption, the evidence, or the speaker's attitude. For Spanish speakers, the typical mistake is omitting these endings or using them interchangeably, which sounds flat or even impolite.
rule:
To achieve near-native fluency in conversation, it is essential to differentiate modal endings based on evidence and shared emotion:

1. **-거든요**: Used to give a reason or information that the speaker assumes the listener does not know, often as justification. It adds a tone of 'you know...' or 'let me tell you...'. It is not used in questions or with commands.

2. **-잖아요**: Indicates that the speaker assumes the listener already knows or should know the fact; introduces a reminder. It can sound challenging if overused.

3. **-더라고요**: Expresses that the speaker discovered or experienced something in the past (sensory evidence or direct experience) and is now sharing it. It contrasts with mere objective observation.

4. **-나 보다 / -ㄴ가 보다**: Used for assumptions based on indirect evidence (what you see, hear, deduce). Equivalent to 'it seems like...', but more natural.

5. **-아/어 보이다, -을/ㄹ 것 같다**: For assumptions based on appearances or impressions.

6. **-는지 알다/모르다**: To express uncertainty within a sentence, similar to 'I don't know if...'.

**Specific pitfalls for Spanish speakers**:
- Not using -거든요 in formal contexts where it is inappropriate; it is typical of colloquial oral register.
- Confusing -더라고요 (past discovery) with -던데요 (description of a situation while sharing it in context).
- Forgetting that -잖아요 can sound condescending if used with superiors.

**Key structures**:
- V-았/었더라고요 (past discovery)
- V-(으)ㄹ 줄 알았어요 (I thought it would...)
- V-는 게 당연하죠 (it's natural that...)
- V-아/아야지요 (should, with a tone of expectation).

concept_examples.text: 그 사람이 벌써 퇴근했나 봐요.
concept_examples.translation: It looks like that person already left work (based on what I see/deduce).
concept_examples.phonetic: [kɯ saram-i pʌlɕ͈ʌ tʰweɡɯnha̠nna bwa̠jo]

concept_examples.text: 어제 그 영화 정말 재미있었더라고요.
concept_examples.translation: Yesterday, that movie was really interesting (I discovered it myself).
concept_examples.phonetic: [ʌdʑe kɯ jʌŋʝwa dʑʌŋmal tɕɛmiitɕ͈ʌt̚tʌɾaɡojo]

concept_examples.text: 내가 그 말을 한 건 다 이유가 있거든요.
concept_examples.translation: Let me tell you that I said that for a reason (that you don’t know).
concept_examples.phonetic: [nɛɡa kɯ maɾɯl ha̠n kʌn ta ijuga it̚k͈ʌdɯnjo]

concept_examples.text: 이미 알고 계시잖아요, 그 프로젝트는 내일 마감이에요.
concept_examples.translation: You already know this, right? The project is due tomorrow.
concept_examples.phonetic: [imi alɡo kjeɕidʑana̠jo, kɯ pʰɯɾoʑɛkt̚ɯn nɛil maɡami ejo]

common_error.explanation: Common among Spanish speakers: using the simple past -었어요 to narrate a personal experience in conversational context without adding the nuance of discovery or sharing an impression. In Spanish, saying 'the movie was interesting' is enough; in Korean, to sound natural and fluent when recounting a past experience you lived through, you use -더라고요 (discovery) or -던데요 (sharing an impression with context). Omitting this ending sounds flat and unidiomatic.

examples.original: 비가 오나 봐요, 우산을 가져가세요.
examples.phonetic: [piɡa ona bwa̠jo, usanɯl kadʑʌɡasejo]
examples.translation: It looks like it’s raining, take an umbrella.
examples.note: Use of -나 보다 for inference based on evidence (clouds, sound). Equivalent to 'it seems like'.

examples.original: 그 식당은 항상 줄 서 있는 걸 보니까 맛있나 봐요.
examples.phonetic: [kɯ ɕikt͈aŋɯn ha̠ŋsa̠ŋ tɕul sʌ inɯn kʌl ponikka̠ ma̠sinna bwa̠jo]
examples.translation: Seeing that there’s always a line at that restaurant, it seems to be good.
examples.note: Combined with -는 걸 보니까 to indicate the basis of the inference.

examples.original: 그 소식 들었어? 아마 사실인가 봐.
examples.phonetic: [kɯ soɕik tɯɾʌssʌ? ama̠ sʰaɕil inɡa bwa̠]
examples.translation: Did you hear that news? It seems to be true.
examples.note: Semi-formal form with -인가 보다, used among friends.

examples.original: 아직 안 왔을 거예요, 길이 막히니까.
examples.phonetic: [adʑik a̠n wa̠sʰɯl kʌjejo, kili ma̠kʰinikka̠]
examples.translation: They probably haven’t arrived yet, because there’s traffic.
examples.note: Use of -을 거예요 for reasoned supposition; in this case, the cause is explicitly stated with -니까.

examples.original: 지난주에 제주도에 갔었는데 정말 좋았더라고요.
examples.phonetic: [dʑina̠ndʑue tɕedʑudo e ka̠s͈ʌnnɯnde dʑʌŋma̠l tɕo̞a̠t̚t͈ʌɾaɡojo]
examples.translation: Last week I went to Jeju and honestly it was really good (let me tell you from experience).
examples.note: -더라고요 adds the nuance of 'I’m sharing an impression I experienced'.

examples.original: 그때는 정말 힘들었던 것 같아요.
examples.phonetic: [kɯt͈e nɯn dʑʌŋma̠l himdɯɾʌt̚t͈ʌn kʌt̚ kka̠tʰa̠jo]
examples.translation: Back then, I think it was really difficult.
examples.note: -었던 것 같아요 for a conjecture about a past memory, softer and more reflective.

examples.original: 아, 맞다! 어제 그 사람이 전화했었더라고요.
examples.phonetic: [a̠, ma̠t̚t͈a̠! ʌdʑe kɯ saram i dʑʌnɦwa̠ɦɛs͈ʌt̚t͈ʌɾaɡojo]
examples.translation: Oh, right! It turns out that person called you yesterday (I found out later).
examples.note: Use of -았었더라고요 for a past discovery you didn’t know at the time.

examples.original: 어릴 때는 그 동네가 참 조용했었는데, 지금은 완전히 달라졌더라고요.
examples.phonetic: [ʌɾil t͈e nɯn kɯ to̞ŋneɡa̠ tɕʰa̠m tɕo̞joŋɦɛs͈ʌnnɯnde, dʑiɡɯmɯn wa̠ndʑʌnhi ta̠lla̠dʑjʌt̚t͈ʌɾaɡojo]
examples.translation: When I was little, that neighborhood was very quiet, but now it’s completely changed (I’ve seen it for myself).
examples.note: Contrast between memory (-었었는데) and current discovery (-더라고요).

examples.original: 제가 말했잖아요, 그렇게 하면 문제가 생긴다고.
examples.phonetic: [tɕeɡa̠ ma̠ɾɦɛt̚tɕ͈a̠na̠jo, kɯɾʌkʰe ha̠mjʌn mundʑeɡa̠ sʰɛŋɡindako̞]
examples.translation: I told you, remember? That if you did that, there would be problems.
examples.note: -잖아요 to appeal to shared knowledge; can sound admonishing if used with a strong tone.

examples.original: 오늘 늦게 온 건 다 이유가 있거든요.
examples.phonetic: [o̞nɯl nɯt̚k͈e o̞n kʌn ta̠ ijuɡa̠ it̚k͈ʌdɯnjo]
examples.translation: The reason I arrived late today is because of something (let me explain).
examples.note: -거든요 to give a justification with information the listener does not possess.

examples.original: 사실 그 프로젝트는 제가 맡게 됐거든요. 그래서 좀 바빠요.
examples.phonetic: [sʰa̠ɕiɭ kɯ pʰɯɾo̞ʑɛk̚t͈ɯnɯn tɕeɡa̠ ma̠t̚k͈e tʰwa̠t̚k͈ʌdɯnjo. kɯɾɛsʰʌ tɕo̞m pa̠p͈a̠jo]
examples.translation: The thing is, I ended up being assigned that project. That’s why I’m a bit busy.
examples.note: Natural use of -거든요 in a longer explanation; creates a connection with the next sentence.

examples.original: 좋은 기회잖아요, 놓치면 후회할지도 몰라요.
examples.phonetic: [tɕo̞ɯn kiɦwe̞dʑa̠na̠jo, no̞tɕʰimjʌn huɦwe̞ɦa̠ʎdʑido̞ mo̞ɭɭa̠jo]
examples.translation: It’s a good opportunity, isn’t it? If you miss it, you might regret it.
examples.note: Combination of -잖아요 to persuade based on something the other already knows, and -ㄹ지도 몰라요 to speculate.
